title: Advection schemes: the same wave, four ways to be wrong
summary: Move a bump or a step across a grid with different spatial schemes and the shape that comes out shows the scheme's character: smeared by numerical diffusion, ringing from dispersion, blown up by instability, or kept bounded by a limiter.

read_the_figure.question: What does each discretization of the advection term do to a profile that should simply translate unchanged?
read_the_figure.axes: Profile figures: x is position on a periodic unit domain, the vertical axis is the transported scalar phi, and the dashed grey line is the initial condition. The exact answer is the initial shape moved along (after one full period it should sit exactly on the dashed line). The space-time figures put x horizontally and time vertically, colour is phi, and a dashed vertical line marks the characteristic x - a t.
look_at: Compare the final curve with the dashed initial or exact curve: lower peak and wider foot means numerical diffusion; extra wiggles or overshoot beyond the initial range means dispersion or instability.

Check the vertical scale before judging a panel. In the scheme-comparison figure the centred-scheme panels run to plus or minus 80 (Gaussian) and about 5e7 (step), so every other panel looks flat only because of that shared scale.
In the step-profile figure, read the printed transition width: the distance over which the front goes from 0 to 1.

In the space-time heatmaps a correct advection is a straight diagonal stripe of constant colour. A stripe that fades along time is damping; the right-hand curve of maximum value against time quantifies it.
In the snapshots, follow the peak height from panel to panel: it falls each time while the shape stays smooth.
read_the_figure.proves: That a scheme does or does not do what its name promises on the simplest transport problem. A scheme that cannot translate a Gaussian cleanly will not carry a flame front, a species or a vortex cleanly either.
if_wrong: Peak falling and base widening: first-order upwind style numerical diffusion, proportional to the grid spacing.
Oscillations growing in time: an unstable combination (here central differences with forward Euler), not merely a dispersive one.
Oscillations that stay bounded and sit next to a sharp front: dispersion of a central or high-order scheme; a limiter is the standard remedy.
Amplitude above the initial maximum with no new source: the scheme is not bounded (not monotone).
must_check: Grid size, CFL number and final time are stated (they are, in the titles and captions).
The same y-axis range or a stated clipping, so scheme panels are comparable.
Whether the exact solution is overlaid. In the profile figures the dashed line is the initial condition, which equals the exact solution only at integer periods.
Limiter or order labels. Some panel labels need care: the centred scheme is labelled dispersive, but at CFL 0.45 with forward Euler the growth shown is instability, see the derivation.
as_drawn: Values read off the figures; approximate unless printed on them.

Scheme comparison (CFL 0.45, t = 1): printed maximum changes are about -0.196 (upwind), +78.8 (centred), -0.004 (TVD minmod), +0.358 (linear upwind) for the Gaussian, and about +4.7e7 for the centred scheme on the step.
Numerical diffusion (step, CFL 0.45, n = 200): printed transition widths 0.130 (upwind), 0.010 (minmod), 0.005 (superbee); the centred panel is saturated with oscillations.
Phase error (sine, CFL 0.4): the titles print 'phase lag about 0.000' for all three schemes, so the visible error is in amplitude (upwind peak about 0.86, centred about 1.10), not phase.
Snapshots (upwind + forward Euler, CFL 0.4, n = 100): peak about 0.79 at t = 1.
Space-time: upwind maximum falls from 1 to about 0.755 by t = 1; minmod from 1 to about 0.989.

terms.meaning: Transport of a quantity by a given velocity a. The model equation is phi_t + a phi_x = 0 and its exact solution just translates the initial shape.
How many cells the wave crosses in one time step. It ties the time step to the grid.
Upwind differencing: the derivative uses the upstream neighbour. First order, bounded, diffusive.
Central differencing: the derivative uses both neighbours. Second order in space, no built-in damping.
A scheme whose total variation cannot grow, so no new extrema appear. A limiter (minmod, superbee) blends first- and second-order fluxes based on local smoothness.
A second-order upwind-biased stencil using two upstream points. See the owner-review note: the figure labels its LUDS curve as an approximation.
Smearing caused by the truncation error of the scheme, behaving like an extra viscosity.
Different wavelengths travelling at different numerical speeds, which produces trailing wiggles.
No new maxima or minima are created. A first-order upwind scheme has it; an unlimited second-order scheme cannot (Godunov's theorem).

remember: Exact advection: phi(x,t) = phi0(x - a t). After one period on a periodic domain the profile must return to where it started.
Upwind: bounded and stable for 0 <= c <= 1, but smears at a rate set by the grid.
Central differencing with forward Euler is unstable at every CFL number.
A limited scheme gets sharp fronts and no overshoot; the price is clipping of smooth peaks.
Read the vertical scale first: a blown-up panel can make good panels look flat.

understand.title: Why upwind smears
understand.text: Expand the upstream difference in a Taylor series and it equals the true derivative plus a second-derivative term with a positive coefficient: the scheme solves an advection-diffusion equation. The extra diffusion is not random: it is proportional to the spacing, so refining the grid shrinks it, slowly.

understand.title: Why central differencing rings
understand.text: Central differencing has no such damping term; its leading error is a third derivative, which makes short waves travel at the wrong speed. A sharp front contains many short waves, so they separate and trail behind as wiggles.

understand.title: Why forward Euler makes it worse
understand.text: Forward Euler is itself slightly anti-diffusive for advection. Added to a central stencil that has no damping to oppose it, every Fourier mode grows by a small factor per step. Small per step, enormous after hundreds of steps.

understand.title: What a limiter does
understand.text: Away from steep gradients it uses the second-order flux (sharp, accurate). Near an extremum or a front it falls back toward upwind (bounded). Minmod limits most (smoother front), superbee least (sharpest front, can square off smooth waves).

steps.title: Exact advection translates the profile
steps.note: Every value travels along a straight characteristic. On the space-time heatmaps this is a diagonal stripe of constant colour.

steps.title: Upwind update as a convex average
steps.note: A weighted average of two old values cannot create a new maximum, so the scheme is bounded. The price is smoothing.

steps.title: Modified equation of upwind with forward Euler
steps.note: Taylor expansion in space and time. The right-hand side is a diffusion term with coefficient D = a dx (1-c)/2, the numerical diffusion.

steps.title: Modified equation of central differencing with forward Euler
steps.note: The same expansion gives a negative diffusion coefficient. A backward diffusion equation is ill-posed, so errors grow. This is the standard explanation of the blown-up centred panels.

steps.title: Amplification factor of central differencing with forward Euler
steps.note: Substitute a Fourier mode. The modulus exceeds one for every mode except the extremes, for any c. The largest growth per step is sqrt(1+c^2).

steps.title: Gaussian width growth under numerical diffusion
steps.note: A diffusing Gaussian conserves its area, so the peak falls as the width grows. This gives a number to check against the snapshot and space-time figures.

steps.title: Width of a smeared front
steps.note: A step under diffusion becomes an error-function profile whose 10 to 90 percent width is 2.56 standard deviations. The printed transition width of the upwind panel can be checked with it.

worked.title: Predict the upwind peak after one period from the numerical diffusion
worked.problem: Upwind + forward Euler, a = 1, n = 100 cells on a unit domain, CFL 0.4, run to t = 1 (the Gaussian is back at its start). The initial Gaussian has standard deviation of about 0.1 (read off the dashed curve in the snapshots figure). Predict the peak height and compare with the 0.79 shown.
worked.answer: About 0.79, matching the peak printed in the t = 1.00 panel. The smearing seen in the figure is fully accounted for by the modified-equation diffusion.

analyze.q: In the scheme-comparison figure the upwind panel looks nearly flat while the centred panel runs to plus or minus 80. Redraw the first panel mentally on its own axis: what would you expect to see, and what does the printed change of -0.196 tell you?
analyze.hint: The peak falls by about 0.2 from 1 to about 0.8; compare with the snapshots.

analyze.q: The phase-error figure prints 'phase lag about 0.000' under every panel yet the title says upwind lags. What is actually different between the three curves, and what would a real phase-error measure be?
analyze.hint: Compare peak heights; a phase measure would be the shift of the zero crossing or of the peak position.

analyze.q: The space-time maximum for minmod falls only from 1 to about 0.989 while upwind falls to 0.755. Why can a second-order-looking limited scheme still lose a little height?
analyze.hint: Limiters clip smooth extrema to stay bounded.

evaluate.q: Which scheme would you choose to advect a smooth temperature bump, and which for a sharp concentration front that must stay between 0 and 1? Justify with panels from the figures.
evaluate.hint: Accuracy on smooth data versus boundedness at fronts.

evaluate.q: Is a figure that clips y to a range where one scheme is saturated a fair comparison? What would make it fairer?
evaluate.hint: Shared axes hide small errors, separate axes hide the relative size.

Sketch the experiment that tells numerical diffusion from physical diffusion: which parameter do you refine, and which curve should converge?

checks.q: Why does upwind smear a Gaussian but keep it bounded?
checks.hint: Write the update as an average.
checks.answer: The update is (1-c) times the old value plus c times the upstream value, an average with non-negative weights for 0 <= c <= 1. An average cannot exceed the largest input, so there is no overshoot. The same Taylor expansion shows a positive diffusion term of size a dx (1-c)/2, which smooths the profile.

checks.q: At a = 1, dx = 0.005 and CFL 0.45, what is the numerical diffusion coefficient of upwind with forward Euler?
checks.answer: D = 0.5 x 0.005 x 0.55 = 0.001375, and sqrt(2 D t) at t = 1 is about 0.052, so the 10 to 90 percent width is about 0.134, close to the 0.130 printed on the upwind panel.

checks.q: A centred-scheme run shows growing wiggles. Is that dispersion or instability, and how do you tell?
checks.hint: Does the amplitude keep growing with time?
checks.answer: Dispersion produces trailing wiggles of roughly fixed size; instability makes the amplitude grow without bound. Here the amplitude reaches tens (Gaussian) and millions (step), which is growth, so it is instability. The amplification factor sqrt(1+c^2 sin^2 theta) is above one.

checks.q: Superbee gives the narrowest front (0.005). Why might you still choose minmod?
checks.answer: Superbee is the most compressive limiter and can steepen smooth waves into staircases. Minmod is the most diffusive of the TVD limiters but keeps smooth data faithful. The choice depends on whether the field is dominated by fronts or by smooth structure.

checks.q: How would you build a test that separates a scheme's diffusion from its dispersion?
checks.answer: Advect a wide Gaussian (mostly long waves, so diffusion shows up as peak loss) and a sine of short wavelength (dispersion shows up as phase lag against the exact translation), for a fixed number of periods, and report peak ratio and phase shift separately.
